articles_and_episodes.title: No Thug’s Veto
articles_and_episodes.summary: by Peter Williams We first heard of the thugs or hecklers veto around 2018 when Canadian speakers Lauren Southern and Stefan Molyneux came to New Zealand. Their attempt to convey opinion at Auckland’s publicly owned Bruce Mason Theatre was stalled for “health and safety concerns”. In other words, those protesting the event would pose too much of a danger for the event to go ahead safely. Somehow the Supreme Court agreed and essentially said while we must allow people to express opinions, it has to be done in a way that doesn’t endanger public safety. So if you don’t like what you’re about to hear, you create such a ruckus that everybody’s in danger – and councils can therefore close public venues to events that protesters don’t like. The case brought about the formation of the Free Speech Coalition, which then developed into the Free Speech Union, which is still going strong today. It was all a very dark time for freedom of expression and freedom of association, but it came to mind again recently when discussion on whether the Maori seats should be abolished in any revised version of our MMP voting system.
